info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 3.1: Manual Imaging, TEI Facsimile, and Document Autopsy.

name.text: 01 Question: From Text to Image: Why Digital Editions Require Facsimiles

questiontext.text: What does publishing the facsimile alongside the transcription do for a reader?

generalfeedback.text: Publishing the image alongside the transcription lets readers check editorial decisions, turning assertions into evidence.

answer.text: It lets them check the editor's decisions against the evidence instead of taking them on trust.

feedback.text: Correct. The image turns editorial claims into something testable.

answer.text: It removes the need for editorial decisions, since readers can read the original themselves.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Most readers still need the transcription; the image lets them audit it.

answer.text: It proves that the transcription is complete and accurate.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It allows verification; it does not by itself guarantee accuracy.

answer.text: It satisfies the copyright requirement to reproduce the source.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Copyright is a separate question, and publishing an image may require permission.

name.text: 02 Question: The TEI `<facsimile>` Element: Structure and Placement

questiontext.text: Where does `` belong in a TEI document, and why?

generalfeedback.text: `` sits between `` and `` as their sibling, keeping physical surfaces separate from transcription.

answer.text: Between `` and `` as their sibling, because a page exists whether or not its words have been transcribed.

feedback.text: Correct. Physical surfaces are kept separate from the transcription.

answer.text: Inside ``, next to ``, because both describe the physical object.

feedback.text: Incorrect. `` describes the object in prose; `` holds image surfaces, outside the header.

answer.text: Inside ``, wrapping the transcribed body it illustrates.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That would tie surfaces to reading order, which is exactly what TEI avoids here.

answer.text: In a separate file, since TEI does not allow images and text in one document.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI holds both in the same root element.

name.text: 03 Question: Modeling Surfaces: The `<surface>` Element

questiontext.text: You are encoding a single-sheet decree printed on both sides. How many `` elements does it need?

generalfeedback.text: Each physical face of the object is one `` with an `xml:id`, which is the handle everything else uses to point at it.

answer.text: Two, because each physical writing face is one surface.

feedback.text: Correct. Front and back are separate faces even though they are one sheet.

answer.text: One, because the whole sheet is a single physical object.

feedback.text: Incorrect. `` models a face, not an object.

answer.text: Four, one for each edge of the sheet.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Edges are not writing faces.

answer.text: As many as there are paragraphs of text on it.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Textual divisions belong in ``, not in the facsimile.

name.text: 04 Question: Coordinates and Space: Declaring Coordinate Systems in `<surface>`

questiontext.text: In ``, what do the last two numbers represent?

generalfeedback.text: `ulx/uly/lrx/lry` are corners with the origin at top-left and y increasing downward, and they describe one particular image file.

answer.text: The lower-right corner, so the image is 4800 pixels wide and 6400 tall with the origin at the top-left.

feedback.text: Correct. They are corners, not width and height, and y increases downward.

answer.text: The width and height of the region, measured from the centre of the image.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI uses corner coordinates measured from the top-left origin.

answer.text: The resolution of the image in pixels per inch, horizontally and vertically.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Resolution is recorded separately; these are coordinates.

answer.text: The lower-right corner, with y increasing upward as in mathematics.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The corner is right, but y increases downward in image coordinates.

name.text: 05 Question: Defining Regions: The `<zone>` Element

questiontext.text: You mark a region on a letter and give it `type="correction"` rather than `type="blot"`. What have you done?

generalfeedback.text: Zones mark meaningful regions inside a surface, and the `@type` you assign is an interpretive claim about the document.

answer.text: Made an interpretive claim about the document, which is an editorial act rather than a technical one.

feedback.text: Correct. Coordinates are measurement; the type is your reading.

answer.text: Chosen between two equivalent labels that carry the same meaning.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They assert different things about what happened on the page.

answer.text: Selected a value that the TEI schema will verify against a fixed list.

feedback.text: Incorrect. `@type` values are not constrained to an enumerated list here.

answer.text: Changed how the zone's coordinates are calculated.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The type has no effect on the geometry.

name.text: 06 Question: Grouping Features: The `<surfaceGrp>` and Sub-surfaces

questiontext.text: A clerk pinned a slip of paper over a corrected clause in a register. How is that modelled?

generalfeedback.text: `` groups related faces and nested surfaces model attached slips, preserving how an object is physically assembled.

answer.text: As a `` nested inside the surface of the page it is attached to, with its own coordinates.

feedback.text: Correct. Nesting models physical attachment, while `` groups related faces such as an opening.

answer.text: As a `` on the page, since the slip covers a region of it.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A zone is an area of one face; the slip is a separate writing surface.

answer.text: As a separate document with its own `` element.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That would lose the physical relationship between slip and page.

answer.text: As a ``, since the slip and the page form a group.

feedback.text: Incorrect. `` groups peers, such as the two pages of an opening.

name.text: 07 Question: Linking Facsimile to Text: The `@facs` Attribute

questiontext.text: What is required for `@facs="#z_line1"` to work, and what will the schema check?

generalfeedback.text: `@facs` links any text element to a surface or zone by its id, and nothing but your own checking confirms the target exists.

answer.text: An element with `xml:id="z_line1"` must exist; the schema checks the value's form but not whether the target is there.

feedback.text: Correct. Dangling pointers validate cleanly, so you must check them yourself.

answer.text: The zone must be defined after the text that points at it, and the schema enforces the order.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Order does not matter, and the schema does not enforce one.

answer.text: The value must be a full URL, and the schema will reject a relative one.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A `#` followed by an id is the normal form.

answer.text: The `@facs` attribute may appear only on ``, and the schema enforces that.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is a global attribute usable on many elements.

name.text: 08 Question: Two-Way Alignment: `<zone>` Pointing to Text and Text Pointing to `<zone>`

questiontext.text: Why does TEI allow zones to point at text as well as text pointing at zones?

generalfeedback.text: Text can point at zones and zones at text, so an edition can be organized around either the words or the object.

answer.text: Because an edition may be organized around the words or around the object, and features like wrapping glosses have a physical position that does not match reading order.

feedback.text: Correct. Two-way linking records both without distorting either.

answer.text: Because `@facs` is deprecated and `@corresp` replaces it.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both are current and serve different purposes.

answer.text: Because some viewers read only one direction, so both must be supplied.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The reason is editorial, not a viewer limitation.

answer.text: Because zones cannot carry `xml:id` values and so must point outward.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Zones require `xml:id` values in order to be referenced.

name.text: 09 Question: The Materiality of the Witness: Media Diversity Across History

questiontext.text: Why does the lesson insist that capture method follows from material?

generalfeedback.text: Every material behaves differently under light and handling, so capture method follows from what the object is made of.

answer.text: Different materials respond differently to light and handling, so a technique that reveals ink on paper can make an inscription disappear.

feedback.text: Correct. Digitization starts by asking what the object is made of and what age has done to it.

answer.text: Because institutions charge different fees for photographing different materials.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The reason is physical, not administrative.

answer.text: Because TEI requires a different element for each writing support.

feedback.text: Incorrect. `` serves all of them; the material is described in the header.

answer.text: Because only parchment and papyrus may be photographed without permission.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Permission depends on the holding institution, not the material.

name.text: 10 Question: Epigraphs and Inscriptions: Stone, Metal, and Three-Dimensional Surfaces

questiontext.text: Why does a flash-lit, head-on photograph of a carved inscription usually fail?

generalfeedback.text: Inscriptions are read through shadow, so they require light raked across the surface rather than aimed at it.

answer.text: The text is depth rather than pigment, and flat light fills the grooves evenly so the letters vanish into the stone.

feedback.text: Correct. Raking light makes the cuts cast shadows, which is what makes them readable.

answer.text: The flash overexposes the pale stone and burns out the lettering.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Even correctly exposed, flat lighting leaves no contrast in the cuts.

answer.text: Stone reflects ultraviolet light, which confuses the camera's sensor.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This is about shadow and relief, not ultraviolet.

answer.text: Inscriptions are usually too large to fit in a single frame.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Size may be a problem, but the lighting failure is the one described.

name.text: 11 Question: Papyri, Ostraca, and Fragile Organic Supports

questiontext.text: Which pair of problems is specific to photographing conserved papyri?

generalfeedback.text: Papyri need diffuse light for fibre texture and polarizers for their protective glass, and their ink flakes rather than fades.

answer.text: Fibre texture that mimics broken strokes, and reflections from the glass plates the fragments are mounted between.

feedback.text: Correct. Diffuse light handles the first and polarizing filters handle the second.

answer.text: Ink that fades under studio light, and paper that yellows on exposure.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Carbon ink does not fade chemically, and papyrus is not paper.

answer.text: Bindings that will not open flat, and shadows in the gutter.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Those are codex problems.

answer.text: Colour casts from iron-gall ink, and cockling from humidity.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Those belong mainly to parchment documents.

name.text: 12 Question: Scrolls and Rotuli: Continuous Writing Surfaces

questiontext.text: What makes a scroll different from a codex for imaging purposes?

generalfeedback.text: Scrolls are captured in overlapping sections under tension-relieving support, never flattened whole.

answer.text: It is a continuous surface rather than a set of pages, and it holds its curl, so it must be captured in sections under supported tension.

feedback.text: Correct. Forcing an old roll flat cracks fibres and detaches ink.

answer.text: It can be laid flat under glass more easily than a bound book.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Flattening a scroll under glass is precisely what must not happen.

answer.text: It has only one writing face, so it needs only one photograph.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A scroll may be metres long and always needs multiple frames.

answer.text: It cannot be modelled in TEI, which assumes page structure.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI can model a scroll as one long surface or a sequence of surfaces.

name.text: 13 Question: Codices, Manuscripts, and Bound Books: Structure and Gutter Shadows

questiontext.text: A bound volume will not open flat, and the inner margin is dark and distorted. What is the correct response?

generalfeedback.text: Bound volumes are photographed in a cradle at a limited opening angle; forcing one flat to remove gutter shadow damages the binding.

answer.text: Use a cradle that holds the book at a limited opening angle and move the camera instead of forcing the book.

feedback.text: Correct. Pressing a binding flat to remove gutter shadow damages sewing and spine.

answer.text: Place a sheet of glass over the opening to hold the pages flat.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is the specific practice the lesson forbids for bound volumes.

answer.text: Increase the exposure until the gutter is as bright as the rest of the page.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That overexposes the rest of the page and does not fix the distortion.

answer.text: Photograph only the outer half of each page, where the text is undistorted.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That discards part of the evidence.

name.text: 14 Question: Broadside Documents, Maps, Prints, and Oversize Sheets

questiontext.text: What are the two main problems with photographing an oversize single sheet?

generalfeedback.text: Oversize sheets need tiled capture or higher resolution and gentle flattening, and they should be described as sheets rather than as codices.

answer.text: Fitting it in the frame without losing resolution, and flattening a folded sheet safely.

feedback.text: Correct. The answers are tiled capture or a higher-resolution camera, plus soft weights in blank margins.

answer.text: Gutter shadow and spine damage.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A single sheet has no gutter or spine.

answer.text: Ink flaking and fibre interference.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Those are papyrus problems.

answer.text: Colour casts and humidity control.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Those apply to all captures, not specifically to oversize sheets.

name.text: 15 Question: Document Handling and Preservation Ethics in the Studio

questiontext.text: Why do conservators now prefer clean, dry hands to cotton gloves for handling paper and parchment?

generalfeedback.text: Preservation outranks capture: clean hands, no snagging jewellery, no forcing, and deliberate page turns.

answer.text: Gloves reduce tactile sensitivity, making tears and creases more likely.

feedback.text: Correct. Gloves remain appropriate for metal, photographs, and surfaces that fingerprints corrode.

answer.text: Gloves transfer lint that contaminates the document surface.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Lint is a minor issue; clumsiness is the documented risk.

answer.text: Gloves are no longer available in most reading rooms.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They are available and still used for specific materials.

answer.text: Skin oils help preserve parchment by keeping it supple.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is not the reason; the reason is control and safety.

name.text: 16 Question: Supporting the Binding: Book Cradles, Foam Wedges, and Straps

questiontext.text: What may be used to hold a curling page flat during an exposure?

generalfeedback.text: Cradles and wedges support the whole leaf at a safe angle, and only inert strips or soft weights in blank margins hold pages still.

answer.text: Clear polyester strips or soft covered weights, placed in blank margins with the least pressure that works.

feedback.text: Correct. Rubber bands, tape, and clips must never touch the object.

answer.text: Low-tack adhesive tape at the corners, removed immediately afterwards.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Adhesives must never be applied to a historical document.

answer.text: A sheet of glass laid across the opening.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Glass presses the binding and abrades flaking surfaces.

answer.text: Paperclips at the outer edge, where there is no text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Clips crease and can rust or cut the leaf.

name.text: 17 Question: Camera Geometry: Sensor Alignment, Focal Plane, and Lens Selection

questiontext.text: Why does keeping the camera parallel to the page matter for your TEI work specifically?

generalfeedback.text: Keep the sensor parallel and centred and use a middle aperture, because tilt distorts every coordinate you later measure.

answer.text: A tilted camera photographs the rectangle as a trapezoid, so measurements and zone coordinates no longer fit the text.

feedback.text: Correct. Keystoning corrupts exactly the measurements the facsimile depends on.

answer.text: A tilt changes the colour balance across the frame.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Tilt distorts geometry; colour comes from lighting and profiles.

answer.text: A tilt prevents the camera from focusing at all.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It can focus, but the plane of focus and the geometry are wrong.

answer.text: A tilt causes the file to be saved at a lower resolution.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Resolution is unaffected by orientation.

name.text: 18 Question: Controlled Illumination: Balanced Studio Lighting and Glare Reduction

questiontext.text: Glare persists on a glossy seal after you reposition the lights. What is the next step?

generalfeedback.text: Two matched lights at 45 degrees give an even field, and cross-polarization removes glare that repositioning cannot.

answer.text: Cross-polarization: polarizing filters on the lights and another on the lens, rotated until the reflection disappears.

feedback.text: Correct. It removes the specular reflection while leaving the text visible.

answer.text: Increase the exposure so the glare is balanced by the rest of the frame.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That brightens everything and does not remove the reflection.

answer.text: Photograph in a darkened room using the camera's flash only.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Direct flash is the most reliable way to create glare.

answer.text: Convert the image to greyscale, which removes specular highlights.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Greyscale conversion does not remove a blown-out reflection.

name.text: 19 Question: Flatbed and Overhead Planetary Scanners: Mechanics and Constraints

questiontext.text: Which document may appropriately be placed face down on a flatbed scanner?

generalfeedback.text: Flatbeds suit stable loose sheets only; bound and fragile material must be captured face up on a support.

answer.text: A stable modern loose sheet.

feedback.text: Correct. Bound and fragile material must be captured face up on a support.

answer.text: A bound register, provided the lid is not pressed down.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Placing a bound volume face down presses the spine regardless of the lid.

answer.text: A papyrus fragment in its glass mount.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Fragile mounted material must not be handled this way.

answer.text: Any document, as long as the scan resolution is set above 600 ppi.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Resolution has nothing to do with whether handling is safe.

name.text: 20 Question: Metric Calibration: Scale Bars and Spatial Resolution (DPI / PPI)

questiontext.text: Why must a scale bar sit at the same height as the document surface?

generalfeedback.text: A coplanar scale bar gives pixels a physical size, and the resulting resolution figure should be recorded with the image.

answer.text: A ruler lower than the raised page is at a different distance from the lens, so measurements taken from it will be wrong.

feedback.text: Correct. The scale is what gives pixels a physical size, so it has to share the page's plane.

answer.text: Otherwise it will be out of focus and unreadable.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Focus is a lesser issue; the measurement error is the point.

answer.text: Otherwise it will cast a shadow across the document.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Shadows are a lighting matter, not the reason for coplanarity.

answer.text: Otherwise the camera cannot calculate white balance correctly.

feedback.text: Incorrect. White balance comes from a grey or colour reference, not the ruler.

name.text: 21 Question: Color Fidelity: Color Calibration Targets and Color Management

questiontext.text: What is the minimum colour practice this lesson asks for, and what does it enable?

generalfeedback.text: Photograph a colour or grey reference under each lighting setup so ageing can later be distinguished from illumination.

answer.text: Include a grey card in the frame under each lighting setup, which allows the cast to be corrected afterwards.

feedback.text: Correct. A full target additionally allows a profile correcting that camera under that light.

answer.text: Set the camera to automatic white balance and trust it.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Automatic settings vary between frames and leave nothing to correct against.

answer.text: Photograph the document twice, under warm and cool light, and average them.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Averaging two casts does not produce a neutral reference.

answer.text: Convert all images to sRGB at capture time.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Converting does not fix a cast introduced by the lighting.

name.text: 22 Question: Environmental Stability: Temperature, Relative Humidity, and Light Exposure

questiontext.text: Why are LED panels the standard lighting for document imaging?

generalfeedback.text: Stable humidity and cool LED light protect the object; keep the lamps off except during the exposure itself.

answer.text: They emit very little heat and no useful ultraviolet, so they do not dry, curl, or fade the object during a session.

feedback.text: Correct. Total exposure still matters, so lights stay off except during the exposure.

answer.text: They render colour more accurately than any other light source.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Colour accuracy comes from calibration; the reason here is physical safety.

answer.text: They are bright enough to allow photography without a tripod.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Stability comes from the copy stand, not the lamp.

answer.text: They can be positioned closer to the page than other lamps.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Proximity is a lighting choice, not the reason for preferring LEDs.

name.text: 23 Question: The Electromagnetic Spectrum in Manuscript Autopsy

questiontext.text: What single fact underlies ultraviolet, infrared, and multispectral imaging?

generalfeedback.text: Inks and supports respond differently across the spectrum, so invisible wavelengths can separate what visible light has merged.

answer.text: Different inks and supports respond differently across the spectrum, so invisible wavelengths can separate what visible light merges.

feedback.text: Correct. Everything in the remaining sections follows from that.

answer.text: Invisible wavelengths penetrate deeper into the page than visible light in every material.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Penetration varies by material; the principle is differential response.

answer.text: Older inks reflect more light than newer ones at all wavelengths.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Age does not produce a uniform change in reflectance.

answer.text: Human vision covers most of the spectrum, so these methods add only marginal detail.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Human vision covers a narrow band, roughly 400 to 700 nanometres.

name.text: 24 Question: Raking Light: Revealing Dry-Point, Ruling, and Surface Topography

questiontext.text: Which evidence does raking light reveal that ordinary photography does not?

generalfeedback.text: Raking light from several directions reveals inkless evidence — ruling, pricking, scratched notes, and erasures.

answer.text: Inkless traces such as ruling, pricking, dry-point notes, and erasures, which have shape but no colour.

feedback.text: Correct. Shoot from several directions, since features run in different orientations.

answer.text: Faded iron-gall ink that has lost its colour.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is a job for ultraviolet or multispectral imaging.

answer.text: Writing on the reverse of the leaf showing through.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Show-through is addressed by two-sided capture and processing.

answer.text: Watermarks embedded in the paper.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Watermarks are usually revealed by transmitted light from behind.

name.text: 25 Question: Reflectance Transformation Imaging (RTI): Mathematical Surface Normal Modeling

questiontext.text: What does RTI provide that a single raking-light photograph does not?

generalfeedback.text: RTI captures dozens of exposures with known light positions, producing a surface you can relight and exaggerate afterwards.

answer.text: A model of the surface that can be relit from any direction afterwards, and exaggerated to show shallow traces.

feedback.text: Correct. The reflective sphere in the frame is what tells the software where each light was.

answer.text: A higher-resolution image of the same surface.

feedback.text: Incorrect. RTI captures shape information, not extra resolution.

answer.text: A colour-accurate record of the ink.

feedback.text: Incorrect. RTI concerns surface shape, and often strips colour to show topography.

answer.text: The ability to see through overlying pigment layers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is infrared reflectography.

name.text: 26 Question: Ultraviolet (UV) Fluorescence: Recovering Erased Iron-Gall Inks and Palimpsests

questiontext.text: Under ultraviolet light, why does erased iron-gall writing appear dark against the parchment?

generalfeedback.text: Under UV, parchment fluoresces while residual iron-gall ink does not, so erased text reappears as dark strokes on a glowing page.

answer.text: The parchment fluoresces while residual iron in the old strokes does not, and suppresses the glow around it.

feedback.text: Correct. The text returns because the surface around it lights up, not because the ink becomes visible.

answer.text: The ink fluoresces brightly while the parchment stays dark.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is the reverse: the parchment glows and the ink quenches it.

answer.text: Ultraviolet light removes the upper layer of text temporarily.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Nothing is removed; the two texts are distinguished optically.

answer.text: The scraped areas are thinner and so transmit more light.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The effect is fluorescence, not transmission.

name.text: 27 Question: Infrared (IR) Reflectography: Penetrating Over-Inking, Soot, and Pigments

questiontext.text: Which situation is infrared reflectography best suited to?

generalfeedback.text: Infrared keeps carbon ink black while many stains and covering inks turn transparent, revealing censored, sooted, or underdrawn text.

answer.text: Text in carbon ink obscured by a covering ink, stain, or soot that becomes transparent under infrared.

feedback.text: Correct. Carbon stays black while many organic materials effectively disappear.

answer.text: Scraped-off writing on parchment with no ink remaining on the surface.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is the classic ultraviolet fluorescence case.

answer.text: Ruling lines scratched into the surface with a hard point.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Inkless topography calls for raking light or RTI.

answer.text: Distinguishing two hands that used the same ink.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Infrared separates materials, not authorship.

name.text: 28 Question: Multispectral and Hyperspectral Imaging: Multi-Band Capture and Spectral Stacks

questiontext.text: What does multispectral imaging capture, and why is it powerful?

generalfeedback.text: Multispectral imaging measures how every point responds across many wavelengths, letting software separate inks that visible light merges.

answer.text: A stack of aligned images across many narrow wavelength bands, so software can combine them to separate inks that look identical in visible light.

feedback.text: Correct. Every point gains a spectral signature, which is what makes the separation possible.

answer.text: A single very high-resolution image combining ultraviolet and infrared exposures.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is a stack of many separate narrow-band exposures, not one blended image.

answer.text: A three-dimensional model of the page's surface relief.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is RTI.

answer.text: A colour-managed reproduction suitable for printing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Its purpose is analysis rather than faithful colour reproduction.

name.text: 29 Question: Archival Capture Workflows: From Sensor to Unprocessed Master

questiontext.text: Which set of habits describes the archival capture workflow?

generalfeedback.text: Shoot raw, keep an unedited TIFF master with its metadata intact, and name files so they identify themselves.

answer.text: Shoot raw where possible, keep an unedited TIFF master with its metadata, and name files systematically.

feedback.text: Correct. It is the same discipline as your Git repository, applied to pixels.

answer.text: Shoot JPEG at maximum quality, edit in place, and keep the camera's original filenames.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Each of these loses either data or the ability to identify the file later.

answer.text: Convert everything to PDF for storage, since it keeps pages together.

feedback.text: Incorrect. PDF recompresses images and is not a preservation master.

answer.text: Strip metadata before archiving, to reduce file size and protect privacy.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Technical metadata is part of the record and should be kept.

name.text: 30 Question: The Digital Surrogate: Integrating Physical Capture into the TEI Edition

questiontext.text: Which header element records how the image was made — equipment, lighting, and resolution?

generalfeedback.text: The facsimile block ties your capture to your encoding, and recording how the image was made completes the chain from object to tag.

answer.text: ``, while `` records what you observed in the object itself.

feedback.text: Correct. Together they let a reader trace the chain from the physical object to the encoded tag.

answer.text: ``, since photography is part of the physical description.

feedback.text: Incorrect. `` describes the object; how the surrogate was produced belongs to ``.

answer.text: ``, which covers how the edition was produced and released.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That element concerns publication and availability.

answer.text: ``, since it holds the images.

feedback.text: Incorrect. `` holds surfaces and coordinates, not capture methodology.
